title: Eschatology
plainLanguageTitle: The end times and eternal destiny

sources.workingBank: ESCH — Dividing Doctrines — Eschatology (Working Bank) v1
sources.friendEdition: ESCH- Dividing Doctrines Question Set v1

sections.title: The Return of Christ

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes your understanding of Jesus Christ’s return?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jesus will personally, visibly, and bodily return in the future.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jesus will return in the future, but primarily in a spiritual or nonbodily sense.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Biblical prophecies of Christ’s return have already been fulfilled.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scripture does not teach a future return of Christ.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

questions.prompt: Must certain prophetic events occur before Christ returns?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  ESCH-01 = A or B

choices.label: A
choices.text: No; Christ could return at any moment without additional events needing fulfillment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes; certain identifiable events must occur first.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some events may remain, but Scripture does not establish a necessary sequence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

questions.prompt: How do you understand the New Testament’s descriptions of Christ coming in glory?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  ESCH-01 = B or C

choices.label: A
choices.text: They describe historical manifestations of divine judgment or kingdom authority.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They describe a future spiritual manifestation rather than a bodily appearance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They combine historical and future spiritual fulfillments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

editorialNotes: Preserve the E-series IDs used in friend comments even though the order differs from the taxonomy.

sections.title: The Intermediate State

questions.prompt: What happens to a person between physical death and the final resurrection?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: The person continues consciously while awaiting bodily resurrection.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The person remains unconscious until resurrection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The person immediately enters their final resurrected existence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scripture does not establish a particular intermediate state clearly.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The whole person dies, with no conscious soul surviving death; God restores the person at resurrection.

choices.label: F
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

choices.label: G
choices.text: I reject the premise of this question

questions.prompt: What happens to believers immediately after death?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  ESCH-02 = A

choices.label: A
choices.text: They enter God’s presence, perfected in holiness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They enter God’s presence but may undergo further purification.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They enter a temporary state of purification before full communion with God.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They consciously rest with Christ while awaiting resurrection; Scripture leaves the question of further purification unresolved.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

questions.prompt: Can someone who dies unreconciled to God subsequently be reconciled to him?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: No; death ends the opportunity for repentance and reconciliation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes; reconciliation remains possible after death.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Scripture does not clearly establish whether this is possible.

editorialNotes: Distinguish the condition of the dead before resurrection from the final state.

sections.title: Resurrection and Final Judgment

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the future resurrection of the dead?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: All human beings, righteous and unrighteous, will be bodily raised.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The righteous will experience bodily resurrection, but the unrighteous will not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Resurrection principally describes spiritual transformation, not a future bodily event for all people.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

questions.prompt: Will the resurrection occur in one event or in distinct stages?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  ESCH-03 = A

choices.label: A
choices.text: One general resurrection of the righteous and unrighteous.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Multiple resurrections separated by identifiable periods or events.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Scripture does not establish the sequence clearly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

questions.prompt: How do you understand the final judgment?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: A future universal judgment in which all humanity appears before Christ.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Multiple future judgments involving different groups or stages.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The language primarily represents God’s judgments within history rather than one future universal event.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Individuals undergo judgment after death, followed by a universal final judgment at the resurrection.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

questions.prompt: How do believers participate in judgment?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  ESCH-03b = A, B, or D

choices.label: A
choices.text: Believers give an account of their lives, but their salvation is secured through Christ.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Believers’ final salvation is evaluated in relation to their faith and deeds.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Believers are exempt from the final judgment entirely.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Believers' judgment concerns reward or loss of reward, not whether they are saved.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

editorialNotes: E3.3 follows choices in E3.2. Opening resurrection selections alone do not govern that question.

sections.title: Eternal Punishment and Reconciliation

questions.prompt: What is the ultimate destiny of those who stand condemned before God?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eternal, conscious punishment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Final destruction, resulting in the end of conscious existence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Punishment or correction that ultimately ends in reconciliation with God.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scripture does not reveal their ultimate destiny with sufficient clarity to affirm one outcome.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The condemned are permanently excluded from God's kingdom, without a settled view on continued consciousness versus destruction.

choices.label: F
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

choices.label: G
choices.text: I reject the premise of this question

questions.prompt: How should biblical descriptions of eternal punishment be understood?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  ESCH-04 = A

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fire, darkness, and torment refer substantially to literal realities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: These descriptions are largely figurative expressions of real, everlasting conscious punishment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Scripture establishes conscious eternal punishment without revealing its precise experiential nature.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

questions.prompt: What makes the punishment everlasting?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  ESCH-04 = B

choices.label: A
choices.text: Its irreversible result: the condemned are ultimately destroyed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The condemned experience conscious punishment that ends in destruction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Scripture does not establish whether destruction is preceded by conscious punishment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

questions.prompt: How certain is universal reconciliation?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  ESCH-04 = C

choices.label: A
choices.text: Scripture teaches that all people will ultimately be reconciled to God.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Universal reconciliation is my hope, but I cannot affirm it as certain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: I believe universal reconciliation is possible, but remain undecided.

questions.prompt: How does final reconciliation occur?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  ESCH-04 = C

choices.label: A
choices.text: Through repentance and reconciliation made possible after death.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Through God’s ultimate restorative judgment, though the process is not clearly revealed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Through Christ's ultimate victory over sin and death, bringing all persons into reconciliation without a separately described postmortem decision.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

editorialNotes: Universal hope, certainty, duration, and the mechanism of reconciliation are distinct convictions.

sections.title: New Heavens and New Earth

questions.prompt: What is the final state of creation and the redeemed?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: God renews and transforms the present creation, where the redeemed live bodily forever.

choices.label: B
choices.text: God replaces the present creation with a wholly new created order, where the redeemed live bodily forever.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The eternal state is principally a nonmaterial heavenly existence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: New creation primarily describes a spiritual reality already being fulfilled.

choices.label: E
choices.text: New creation is already inaugurated in Christ and will be consummated in a future bodily renewal of creation.

choices.label: F
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

questions.prompt: How should descriptions of the New Jerusalem and renewed creation be understood?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  ESCH-05 = A or B

choices.label: A
choices.text: Primarily as descriptions of actual future places and conditions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Primarily as symbolic descriptions of a real future embodied existence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: As a combination of literal and symbolic realities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

questions.prompt: Will the redeemed continue meaningful activity in the new creation?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  ESCH-05 = A or B

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes; work, stewardship, relationships, and worship will continue in redeemed forms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eternity will primarily consist of worship and communion with God, without necessarily retaining earthly activities.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Scripture does not specify enough to determine this.

editorialNotes: The friend edition directs E5.1 and E5.2 to A/B. E also affirms future renewal. Review whether readers choosing E should see those follow-ups in a future revision.

sections.title: The Millennium

questions.prompt: How do you understand the thousand-year reign described in Revelation 20?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: Christ returns before a future reign on earth, during which the millennium takes place.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Christ returns after an era in which the gospel and his kingdom achieve widespread influence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The millennium symbolizes Christ’s present reign until his return, without requiring a distinct future era of worldwide gospel ascendancy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The thousand years should not be fitted into any of these chronological frameworks.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The millennium is already underway, and Christ's present reign will culminate in an era of widespread gospel flourishing before his return.

choices.label: F
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

questions.prompt: Must the millennium last exactly one thousand calendar years?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  ESCH-06 = A

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes; the duration is literal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No; the thousand years represents an extended but not necessarily exact period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Scripture does not establish whether the number is literal.

questions.prompt: How should the first resurrection in Revelation 20 be understood?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: A future bodily resurrection occurring before the millennial reign.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Spiritual regeneration or participation in Christ’s resurrection life.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The heavenly life and reign of departed believers with Christ.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

questions.prompt: What do you expect to happen to the gospel’s influence before Christ returns?
questions.displayNote: Common follow-up  |  All readers of this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: It will progressively transform nations and societies on a widespread scale.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It will advance significantly, but righteousness and opposition will continue until Christ returns.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The world will experience increasing rebellion and opposition to Christianity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scripture does not establish a predictable global trajectory.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

questions.prompt: What future role, if any, does national or ethnic Israel have in God’s promises?
questions.displayNote: Optional depth  |  Available by choice

choices.label: A
choices.text: Israel retains a distinct prophetic future and covenantal role alongside the church.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Israel has a promised future conversion or restoration within the one people of God.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The promises are fulfilled in Christ and his people without requiring a distinct future national fulfillment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Israel will experience a future national or territorial restoration, but has no separate way of salvation or covenant membership apart from Christ.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

editorialNotes: E6.4 is optional and overlaps the Israel dimension in COV. Reuse the answer when possible.

sections.title: Tribulation and Rapture

questions.prompt: How do you understand the great tribulation described in biblical prophecy?
questions.displayNote: Foundational  |  On entry to this dimension

choices.label: A
choices.text: It primarily refers to events fulfilled in the first century.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It describes suffering and persecution throughout the church age.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It primarily refers to a distinct period of intensified suffering still to come.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It has historical and recurring fulfillments, possibly culminating in a final tribulation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It does not describe an identifiable historical period.

choices.label: F
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

questions.prompt: How do you understand the gathering of believers to Christ in 1 Thessalonians 4?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  ESCH-01 = A or B

choices.label: A
choices.text: Believers are gathered to Christ in an event distinct from and earlier than his public return.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Believers are gathered to Christ as part of his one public return.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The passage primarily describes spiritual realities, rather than a literal future gathering.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only some believers will be gathered before Christ's public return, with other believers gathered later (a partial-rapture view).

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

questions.prompt: When does the initial gathering occur relative to a future tribulation?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  ESCH-07a = A or D

choices.label: A
choices.text: Before the tribulation begins.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Around the midpoint of the tribulation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: After significant tribulation, but before the final outpouring of divine wrath.

choices.label: D
choices.text: At the conclusion of the tribulation, shortly before Christ’s public appearance.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The gathering is separate, but its timing is unknown.

choices.label: F
choices.text: I reject the premise of this question

questions.prompt: Will the church experience it?
questions.displayNote: Conditional follow-up  |  ESCH-07 = C, or ESCH-07 = D with a future tribulation affirmed

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes; the church will endure the tribulation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No; the church will be removed before the tribulation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The church will experience part of it but be delivered before its conclusion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The church will remain on earth through the tribulation but will be protected from divine wrath without being removed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

editorialNotes: E7.1 draws on E1, not E7. In E7.3, ask readers choosing E7-D whether their answer actually includes a future tribulation.

questions.prompt: Which approaches best describe how you interpret Revelation’s visions?
questions.displayNote: Optional depth  |  Available by choice

choices.label: A
choices.text: Many visions principally describe events in the first century.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The visions trace events across the history of the church.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many visions principally describe events still future.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The visions portray recurring spiritual realities and conflicts throughout history.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Different sections require different interpretive approaches.

choices.label: F
choices.text: Unsure / I don't know enough yet

editorialNotes: Question IDs, answer choices, and existing review flags follow the current Friend Feedback edition. Use the dimension headings to enter any topic. For a guided reading, continue to the next main question after each applicable branch.

An opening question starts its topic. A common follow-up is available to all readers of that topic. Conditional follow-ups use the answer letters shown. Optional depth is by choice, and uncertainty alone never triggers a doctrinal inference.

vocabulary.definition: The study of last things, including Christ’s return, resurrection, judgment, and the destiny of creation.
A New Testament term for arrival or presence, commonly used in theology for Christ’s coming.
The condition of the dead between bodily death and the final resurrection.
In Catholic theology, the final purification after death of people who die in God’s friendship and will enter heaven.
God’s raising of the dead to embodied life.
God’s ultimate judgment of humanity, in which Christ discloses and judges human lives.
The view that the wicked ultimately cease to exist as persons under divine judgment.
The final reconciliation of all people to God through Christ, which Christians may affirm as certain, hope for, or reject.
The view that those finally condemned remain conscious and experience divine punishment without end.
The thousand-year reign described in Revelation 20, interpreted differently as to timing, nature, and duration.
The view that Christ will return before a future millennial reign.
The view that Christ will return after a period in which the gospel and his kingdom achieve widespread influence.
The view that Revelation’s millennium signifies Christ’s reign in the present age leading up to his return.
The catching up of believers to meet Christ, described in 1 Thessalonians 4, with differing views of its timing and relationship to his return.
Severe distress described in biblical prophecy, with differing views on when it occurs and whom it concerns.
